{{Short description|Region between parallel planes intersecting a sphere}}
{{inline |date=May 2024}}
[[File:LaoHaiKugelschicht1.png|thumb|A spherical segment]]
[[File:01sphere2planes.pdf|thumb|Pair of parallel planes intersecting a sphere forming a spherical segment (i.e., a spherical frustum)]]
[[File:02sph.seg.3D.pdf|thumb|Terminology for spherical segments.]]

In [[geometry]], a '''spherical segment''' is the [[solid (geometry)|solid]] defined by cutting a [[sphere]] or a [[ball (mathematics)|ball]] with a pair of [[Parallel (geometry)|parallel planes]].
It can be thought of as a [[spherical cap]] with the top truncated, and so it corresponds to a '''spherical [[frustum]]'''. 

The [[surface (mathematics)|surface]] of the ''spherical segment'' (excluding the bases) is called '''spherical zone'''.

[[File:Geometric parameters for spherical segment.pdf|thumb|Geometric parameters for spherical segment.]]

If the [[radius]] of the sphere is called {{mvar|R}}, the radii of the spherical segment bases are {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b}}, and the height of the segment (the distance from one parallel plane to the other) called {{mvar|h}}, then the [[volume]] of the spherical segment is

: <math>V = \frac{\pi}{6} h \left(3 a^2 + 3 b^2 + h^2\right).</math>

For the special case of the top plane being tangent to the sphere, we have <math>b = 0</math> and the solid reduces to a [[spherical cap]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kern |first1=Willis |last2=Bland |first2=James |title=Solid Mensuration with Proofs |date=1938 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Inc |location=New York |pages=97-103 |edition=Second |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.205959 |access-date=16 May 2024}}</ref>

The equation above for volume of the spherical segment can be arranged to
: <math>V = \biggl [ \pi a^2 \left (\frac{h}{2} \biggr ) \right ] + \biggl [ \pi b^2 \left ( \frac{h}{2} \biggr ) \right ] + \biggl [ \frac{4}{3} \pi \left( \frac{h}{2} \right)^3 \biggr ]</math>

Thus, the segment volume equals the sum of three volumes: two right circular cylinders  one of radius {{mvar|a}} and the second of radius {{mvar|b}} (both of height <math>h/2</math>) and a sphere of radius <math>h/2</math>.

The curved [[surface area]] of the spherical zone—which excludes the top and bottom bases—is given by

: <math>A = 2 \pi R h.</math>

Thus the surface area of the segment depends only on the distance between the cutting planes, and not their absolute heights.
